question.value: Systematically identify the massive cores in W43-MM1 which contain a hot core and compare their temperature and molecular composition.

evidence.quote: We aim to systematically identify the massive cores which contain a hot core and compare their molecular composition.

claims.hypothesis: Hot cores in W43-MM1 can be systematically identified without prior line identification by mapping summed COM brightness temperatures or measuring line-to-continuum fractions in continuum cores.
claims.experiment: Mapped the pixel-by-pixel mean line brightness temperature in the COM-rich 233 GHz Band 6 spw7 window, calculated core-averaged line contributions (C_Lines^core) and line channel fractions (F_Lines^core) across 9 spectral windows, and compared them to CH3OCHO and CH3CN integrated emission maps.
claims.result: All methods consistently identify the same 8 hot cores: 7 massive cores (#1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10 with masses 16-100 M_sun) and 1 lower-mass core (#11, 2 M_sun).
claims.finding: W43-MM1 is rich in massive hot cores, and blind line-richness metrics reliably identify the same hot cores as targeted COM maps.

evidence.quote: W43-MM1 turns out to be a region rich in massive hot cores. It contains at least 1 less massive (core #11, 2 M$_\odot$) and 7 massive (16 to 100 M$_\odot$) hot cores.

evidence.loc: Comparison of the hot cores identification methods
evidence.quote: The two methods described in Sect. 3.3 and 3.4 succeed in identifying the same hot cores.

evidence.loc: Identification from the spatial distribution of CH$_3$OCHO and CH$_3$CN
evidence.quote: The methyl formate map highlights the eight hot cores identified on Fig. 2.

claims.hypothesis: CH3CN and CH3CCH K-ladder transitions trace different temperature regimes and spatial zones of the protostellar cores.
claims.experiment: Performed LTE MCMC modelling with CASSIS on beam-averaged spectra of CH3CN, CH3(13)CN, CH3CN v8=1 (J=5-4), and CH3CCH (J=6-5) in Band 3 for the 8 hot cores.
claims.result: CH3CN excitation temperatures are 120-160 K across all 8 hot cores, whereas CH3CCH excitation temperatures are 50-90 K with smaller linewidths.
claims.finding: CH3CN traces the warm inner hot core (around 150 K) where ices sublimate, while CH3CCH preferentially traces the cooler outer envelope.

evidence.quote: The excitation temperature of CH$_3$CN, whose emission is centred on the cores, is of the same order for all of them (120–160 K).
In contrast, CH$_3$CCH emission is found to preferentially trace more the envelope, with a temperature ranging from 50 K to 90 K.
The difference of temperatures between CH$_3$CN (120-160 K) and CH$_3$CCH (50-90 K) suggests that CH$_3$CCH traces the outer envelope whereas CH$_3$CN traces the inner part.

claims.hypothesis: The hot cores in W43-MM1 share a similar chemical composition and excitation despite spanning more than an order of magnitude in core mass.
claims.experiment: Rescaled the hot core spectra using three CH3OCHO doublets (intensity factors spanning 1 to 29.1) and performed channel-by-channel linear correlations and intensity ratio analyses against reference core #3 in the 233 GHz COM-rich band.
claims.result: After scaling, the spectral line intensities across the 8 hot cores agree within a factor of 2-3, and CH3OCHO scaling factors correlate linearly with the spectrum-spectrum regression slopes.
claims.finding: The hot cores have a very similar chemical composition and excitation of most COMs, likely formed on similar filament ices prior to desorption.

evidence.quote: There is a factor of up to 30 difference in the intensity of the complex organic molecules (COMs) lines. However the molecular emission of the hot cores appears to be the same within a factor 2–3.

For all sources $R_i$ remains close to 1 within a factor 3, and in many cases within a factor 2, for most channels $i$ where the core #3 spectrum is above 2 K (core #3 maximum intensity being about 12.9 K); these limits are indicated respectively by the green and red horizontal lines.
The 2–3 factor of agreement between the spectra suggests a similar molecular composition of the cores, which can be due to the formation of the molecules.

claims.hypothesis: O-bearing COM emission in core #2 is associated with protostellar outflows rather than solely radiatively heated central core gas.
claims.experiment: Imaged the blue- and red-shifted velocity components of methyl formate (CH3OCHO) at 0.24'' (~1300 au) resolution using uniform weighting and compared their spatial distribution with CO and SiO outflow lobes.
claims.result: The blue and red components of CH3OCHO (and CH3OH, OCS) are offset from the dust continuum center and spatially coincide with the blue and red outflow lobes.
claims.finding: O-bearing COMs in core #2 are at least partially released from ice mantles via shock sublimation or UV irradiation along the outflow cavity walls.

evidence.quote: In core #2, the emission of O-bearing molecules, like OCS, CH$_3$OCHO and CH$_3$OH, does not peak at the dust continuum core center; the blue and red shifted emission correspond to the outflow lobes, suggesting a formation via the sublimation of the ice mantles through shocks or UV irradiation on the walls of the cavity.

evidence.loc: Methyl formate as a tracer of hot cores
evidence.quote: Figure 12 presents the spatial distribution, on a higher resolution (0.24$\ensuremath{''}$ or $\sim$1300 au), of the blue and red components of the methyl formate lines for core #2. These components do not peak at the continuum center and their positions coincide with the blue and red parts of the outflows as traced by the CO and SiO emission (cite: nony20).

why_this_data.value: W43-MM1 hosts a large number of massive cores at 2000 au scales, making it an ideal laboratory to study massive star formation; Band 6 spw7 (~2 GHz around 233 GHz) is rich in COM lines without strong contamination from simple molecules, while Band 3 covers the K-ladders of thermometer molecules CH3CN and CH3CCH at matched ~0.46'' resolution.

evidence.quote: The large number of massive cores detected in W43-MM1 make it an ideal laboratory for understanding the physical processes and chemical evolution involved in the formation of massive stars.

evidence.loc: Hot core identification from the spatial distribution of COMs
evidence.quote: To highlight the presence of hot cores, we focus on the analysis of the “continuum” band (spw7) at 233 GHz, because this band offers a large band width ($\sim$ 2 GHz) not contaminated by strong emission lines coming from the simplest molecules (like H$_2$CO, CO or SiO) but mainly by COMs.

Methyl cyanide (CH$_3$CN) and methyl acetylene (CH$_3$CCH) are considered as two good thermometers, as long as the lines are optically thin, because their emission K-ladder lines are close in frequency and cover a large enough range of upper level energies $E_{\rm u}$ (cite: giannetti17).

why_this_method.value: Pixel-based and core-integrated COM line richness methods identify hot cores without requiring prior line identification or core velocity determinations; scaling by CH3OCHO doublets and channel-by-channel correlation plots allow quantitative comparison of chemical composition without lengthy full physical/chemical modelling of every line.

evidence.quote: To identify hot cores, we used two different approaches, one which uses molecules known to trace hot cores (see Sect. 3.5) and another one which does not need any line identification and which relies on the richness of the hot core spectra in COM lines.
The MF doublets transitions have similar $E_{\rm u}$ levels (99 to 109 K) and are therefore most probably tracing the same volume of gas.

A full modelling of each source in terms of physical structure and chemical composition would be the ideal approach but it is a lengthy process. We propose here a preliminary simpler approach to start quantifying the similarity of the cores based on correlation plots of each source spectrum with that of a reference source.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Full physical structure and chemical composition modelling of all lines in every core was considered ideal but deferred as too lengthy in favour of CH3OCHO scaling and spectrum-spectrum correlation plots.

evidence.quote: A full modelling of each source in terms of physical structure and chemical composition would be the ideal approach but it is a lengthy process. We propose here a preliminary simpler approach to start quantifying the similarity of the cores based on correlation plots of each source spectrum with that of a reference source.

limitations_admitted.value: Up to 11 of the 131 continuum cores from Motte et al. (2018), including outflow-associated core #15 which has detectable molecular lines, lie near or outside the mosaic borders and are excluded from the cleaned field and analysis.

evidence.quote: Hence, 120 to 129 out of the 131 cores of are in the cleaned field, depending on the band.

Note that, as indicated in Sect. 2, up to 11 of the 131 cores from are out of the bounds of our data-cubes. Specifically, this is the case of cores #15, 39, 44, 59 and 67 located in W43-MM1 SW, all of them associated with molecular outflows (cite: nony20).

limitations_admitted.value: Direct individual analysis of cores #1 and #4 is difficult because they appear to be in interaction and suffer from significant spectral confusion.

evidence.loc: Hot core identification from the spatial distribution of COMs
evidence.quote: A direct analysis for cores #1 and 4 is difficult because they appear to be in interaction and affected by significant spectral confusion.

limitations_admitted.value: The relative line contribution metric C_Lines^core is biased by noise at low continuum intensities.

evidence.loc: Hot core identification from the line densities in continuum cores
evidence.quote: Note that the rapid increase of the relative line contribution at low continuum values corresponds to the cores fainter in lines, for which the method is biased by the noise (blue areas).

limitations_admitted.value: The CH3CN temperature modelling assumes a simple uniform source where CH3CN, CH3(13)CN, and CH3CN v8=1 arise from the same region.

evidence.quote: We assume here a simple model with a uniform source and the emission of CH$_3$CN, CH$_3^{13}$CN and CH$_3$CN $\varv_8$=1 coming from the same region. A more realistic source model will be used in a forthcoming paper.

referee_caveats_inferred: The 3 mm Band 3 data reduction is explicitly described as preliminary prior to the standardised ALMA-IMF pipeline release (Cunningham et al.).
Uncertainties on column densities, linewidths, and source sizes in Table 2 are not reported (only a general +/- 20 K uncertainty on CH3CN T_ex is stated).

Assuming identical spatial sizes and co-spatial emission for ground-state CH3(13)CN (E_u = 13-128 K) and vibrationally excited CH3CN v8=1 (E_u = 532-706 K) may bias the derived excitation temperatures and source sizes.

reproducibility.score_reason: The ALMA project codes, spectral windows, beam sizes, noise levels, target coordinates, spectroscopic constants, and mathematical formulas for the line-richness and correlation metrics are clearly documented, and the main results are numeric. However, low-level imaging/calibration parameters and exact CASSIS MCMC priors are omitted or deferred to companion papers.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: All three ALMA project codes are public in the archive, the core coordinates and rest frequencies are tabulated in full, the equations for line-richness metrics and spectral correlation are explicit, and the derived temperatures, column densities, scaling factors, and correlation slopes provide clear numeric answer keys.
